title: Neural networks, and reusing pretrained ones
hook: Train from scratch, fine-tune, use as-is, or extract features. Almost nobody starts from zero.
inPlainWords: A neural network learns by guessing, checking, and nudging itself, over and over, across many examples. The big idea: a network that already learned general things, like edges, shapes and word meaning, can be reused for your task.

useCase.title: Sort 2,000 labeled product photos into 30 categories
useCase.story: ShopEase has 2,000 photos, labeled by hand, across 30 categories. The photos come from different phones and lighting. The team is three people with one small GPU.

approaches.name: Train from scratch
approaches.greatWhen: You have millions of examples, or unusual data that no pretrained model has seen.
approaches.example: Training an image network on 2,000 photos alone.

approaches.name: Use a pretrained model as it is
approaches.what: Use a model someone already trained, without changing it.
approaches.greatWhen: Your categories match what it already knows.
approaches.example: A general image model tags shoe, bag and lamp.

approaches.name: Feature extraction
approaches.what: Use the pretrained network to turn each image into numbers, then train a small classic model on those.
approaches.greatWhen: Small data, and you want it fast with no GPU training.
approaches.avoidWhen: You need the very best accuracy.
approaches.example: Image to numbers, then a simple classifier.

approaches.name: Fine-tuning (transfer learning)
approaches.what: Start from a pretrained network and train it a little on your photos.
approaches.greatWhen: You have hundreds to thousands of examples per category. This is the usual best choice.
approaches.avoidWhen: You have almost no labeled data.

approaches.name: Prompt a hosted vision model
approaches.what: Send images to a hosted vision model and describe the categories in the prompt.
approaches.greatWhen: No training team, low volume, or categories that change often.
approaches.example: "Which of these 30 categories fits this photo?"

challenge.question: 2,000 labeled photos, 30 categories, three people, one small GPU. What do you do?

options.why: 2,000 photos are far too few to learn vision from nothing.

options.text: Fine-tune a pretrained vision model on the photos
options.why: It already knows edges, textures and shapes. Your photos only teach it your 30 categories.
Costly, and unnecessary when a pretrained model exists.

options.text: Extract features and train a simple classifier
options.why: A great quick baseline, but fine-tuning usually reaches higher accuracy.

bestCase.title: Start from a pretrained network and adapt it
bestCase.example: The pretrained model already knows edges, textures and shapes. Fine-tuning on 2,000 photos takes an afternoon and reaches good accuracy. A quick feature-extraction baseline was built first to know the bar.

worstCase.title: Training from scratch on a small set
worstCase.example: A blank network memorizes the 2,000 photos, including the photographer's desk in the background. It works on the training photos and fails on new lighting and new angles.

route.travelling: Photo of a red trainer on a desk

steps.label: Pick a pretrained model
steps.goes: Choose one already trained on millions of images.
steps.goesWrong: The team starts with a blank network. It has no general knowledge to reuse.

steps.label: Add a new final layer
steps.goes: A small new part maps its knowledge to your 30 categories.

steps.label: Fine-tune gently
steps.goes: Train a little on your own photos.

steps.label: Check on unseen photos
steps.goes: Accuracy holds up on different phones and lighting.

takeaway: Do not train from zero. Reuse what a pretrained network already knows, and adapt it.
